editorial: The title promises every signal, but logs were turned off and no HTTP metrics appeared. The post shows traces, the service map, and JVM and connection pool metrics only. Fix: Retitle to match what was shown and credit the product, for example: 'One Env Var, a Full Service Map in Splunk APM: What the OTel Java Agent Costs at Startup'. Drop 'every signal' from the TL;DR as well.

technical: The Build section says the wrong script installs the Collector. reproduce.sh installs it so that it runs in both measurements; fix.sh never calls helm. Fix: Move the helm block to Step 2 and say the Collector runs in both runs, so the agent is the only difference. Step 3 becomes 'Attach the agent and measure again'.

technical: The memory claim isn't supported. The heap is set with -Xms256m, but RSS only counts heap pages that have been touched, so some of the added 92 to 94 MiB may be heap. The lab doesn't split heap from non-heap memory. Fix: Either remove the 'outside -Xmx' clause, or add a jcmd VM.native_memory summary (or jvm.memory.used split by heap and non-heap from Splunk) in both runs and report the split.

technical: The startup table reports one number per cell, with no samples, no versions and no CPU context. +18 s is the headline cost, and it comes from 3 samples with both JVMs starting together on a t3.large with a 100m CPU request. Fix: Label the column as the median of 3 and list all six samples per service from startup-before.txt and startup-after.txt. State the agent version (v2.33.1), Spring Boot 3.5.6, Java 21 and the CPU request. Say plainly that the figure includes CPU contention from two JVMs starting at once.

editorial: The opening counts '3 services on the map', but only two services run the agent. The third is Postgres, which Splunk APM inferred. Fix: Write '2 instrumented services plus Postgres, which Splunk APM inferred from the client spans'. It is accurate, and the inferred node is a better product point than a bare count.

editorial: The post doesn't compare its result with what was already known, so readers can't tell whether 18 s is normal. The brief cites issue 8629 as existing coverage, but the post never mentions it. Fix: Add one paragraph setting this lab's +18 s on an 11.5 s base next to the issue's +23.5 s on a 61 s base. Present any 'roughly fixed cost' reading as a hypothesis for a follow-up run, not as a finding, and link the issue.
outside claim without a known source: I work at Splunk, part of Cisco; the post isn't sponsored or reviewed by my employer.

The core measurements are real and the before-check could fail. The fix.sh script checks the cluster's 801 time series before it counts agent metric names, so a zero there means no application telemetry, not a broken path.

The Build section says fix.sh installs the Collector. The lab code shows reproduce.sh installs it (chart 0.163.1) and fix.sh never runs helm. A reader following the steps will misread which run had the Collector.

Two claims go beyond the evidence. 'The added 92 to 94 MiB sits outside your -Xmx setting' is not shown, because VmRSS also counts heap pages the agent touches. Each startup figure is a median of 3 restarts, with both JVMs starting together on one burstable node with a 100m CPU request. The post doesn't show the samples or say how much CPU each JVM got.
The post never names the agent version (v2.33.1), Spring Boot 3.5.6, Java 21 or the Collector chart in the results. Readers can't compare these numbers with issue 8629 or with later releases.
The reader and the decision are clear, and the cost table is the useful part. A measured +18 s startup on an 11.5 s service is something the docs don't tell a platform engineer.
The title says 'Every Signal', but logs were turned off and no http.* metrics appeared. The post admits both at the end, so the headline promises more than was shown.

The structure reads as generated: 'The trick:', 'The proof:', 'Here's exactly what appeared', a bolded TL;DR, and an even, section-by-section rhythm. The opening line 'Every Java team asks two questions' is stock phrasing.
The strongest finding is buried. Startup, not latency, is the cost to plan for. The post could set it next to the issue 8629 report (+23.5 s on a 61 s app), but it never mentions that issue.
The brief rates demand as weak. It has about six participants on one issue, an 11-reply discussion and an open PR. There is no search or view data, so this can't score above 3.
'Every Signal ... With Zero Code' is not how people phrase the problem. The threads ask about agent startup time and CPU overhead. A title built on the startup number would match their words.
Splunk fits naturally here: the service map, the inferred Postgres node and the trace lookup are real reasons to read it.

claims.text: Every Java team asks two questions before an agent goes near their service: what do I get, and what will it cost me?
The heap was fixed at 256 MiB, so the added 92 to 94 MiB sits outside your -Xmx setting.
Hand-written spans can follow for business steps it can't know about.
Give your startup probes room before you roll out.

brief.reader: Platform engineer rolling out observability to Java teams on Kubernetes
brief.decision: Whether to turn on the OTel Java agent everywhere first, before asking any team for code changes
brief.question: What exactly do I get in Splunk Observability Cloud from the OTel Java agent alone, and what does it cost my service?
brief.takeaway: You can show a team its service map, traces and JVM and HTTP metrics from one environment variable, and quote measured startup, memory and p95 numbers when they ask what it costs.
brief.adds: Existing pages list what the agent can emit and how to tune overhead, and one issue reports older startup numbers. This post shows what one small Spring Boot system really produced in Splunk, and measures startup, memory and p95 on the same jar, image and Collector with the current agent.
brief.open_question: With one environment variable and no code change, how many services, metric names and spans per request does the OTel Java agent put in Splunk Observability Cloud, and how much startup time, memory and p95 latency does it add to a Spring Boot service?
tradeoffs: Agent on every service first, or hand-written instrumentation later
Default settings, or tuning instrumentation and sampling for lower overhead
Traces and metrics reach Observability Cloud here; application logs follow a separate route

existing_pages.title: Startup performance is downgraded significantly when add opentelemetry agent in spring project
existing_pages.covers: One report of startup averages with and without older agent versions. It has no Kubernetes or memory figures, and shows no Splunk result.

demand.evidence: Three real threads in the OTel Java instrumentation repo. An issue reports Spring startup rising from 61.4s to 84.9s on average with the agent, with about six participants. A 2024 discussion with 11 replies asks about high CPU during startup, and a maintainer advises estimating overhead and reserving resources. PR 21033, ready for review since 29 Oct 2026, reports a 5.19% cut in agent-added startup. No search volume data was available.
